headline_en: Career opportunities in Ireland for Bangladeshi doctors and nurses; three exams
summary_en: A feature by Syed Atiqur Rob explains why few Bangladeshi doctors and almost no Bangladeshi nurses work in Ireland despite Ireland's heavy reliance on foreign health workers. It sets out the registration steps (IMC registration, PRES exam or PLAB/MRCP alternative, IELTS/OET), the barriers (degree recognition, no government agreement, no sponsorship channel or recruiters), pay ranges, and what the writer says Bangladesh should do.

facts.statement: According to 2023 figures cited in the article, about 40 percent of all doctors working in Ireland are foreign.
According to 2023 figures cited in the article, about 51.8 percent of Ireland's nursing workforce was trained abroad.

The Irish Medical Council (IMC) recognises (the article says 'easily recognises') medical degrees from India, Pakistan, the Philippines and Egypt, but recognition is hard to get for Bangladeshi degrees, so Bangladeshi doctors face extra exams that are time-consuming and costly.

Ireland's nursing board (NMBI) recognises nurses from the Philippines, India and Nigeria because it has formal agreements with those countries; there is no such agreement with Bangladesh, so Bangladeshi nurses who apply face various complications.

The article says Bangladeshi doctors in Ireland are very few and Bangladeshi nurses almost non-existent; most Bangladeshi doctors working in Ireland come there from various Middle Eastern countries. Thousands of health workers from India, Pakistan, the Philippines, Egypt, Sudan and Nigeria work in Ireland.
Step 1 for a Bangladeshi doctor to work in Ireland: register with the Irish Medical Council (IMC); registration depends on the doctor's experience and educational qualifications.
Step 2: if the medical degree is not recognised, the doctor must sit PRES (Pre-Registration Examination System), which includes a written exam, a clinical skills exam and a supervised internship.

Alternative route: a doctor who has passed PLAB or MRCP can get IMC registration without the PRES exam. To work as a specialist, CESR (Certificate of Eligibility for Specialist Registration) or an equivalent qualification is required.
Even after passing PRES, a language test (IELTS or OET) is mandatory for IMC registration. Doctors and nurses need at least IELTS 7.0 or OET grade 'B' to work in Ireland.
The article says the Philippines, India, Nigeria and Sudan have formal health-worker supply agreements with Ireland, so their doctors and nurses are approved easily; Bangladesh has no such agreement.

Applying directly to an Irish hospital requires sponsorship, which the article says is quite hard for Bangladeshis to get. India and other countries have specific recruitment agencies that connect with Irish hospitals; there is nothing like that for Bangladeshis.
The article says demand in Ireland for specialist doctors is very high, especially in anaesthesia, cardiology, neurology and surgery.

Ireland runs a special employment programme called the 'Critical Skills Employment Permit' through which certain professionals easily get work permission; the writer says that if Bangladesh could be included in it, entry for doctors and nurses would be easier.

Pay in Ireland as stated in the article: an entry-level doctor can earn about 50,000 to 60,000 euros a year; specialist doctors 120,000 to 200,000 euros; consultant-level doctors can earn more than 210,000 euros.
Nurses' pay in Ireland as stated in the article: about 30,000 euros a year at entry level, and can exceed 55,000 euros at senior level.

The writer recommends that the Bangladesh government negotiate degree recognition with the IMC and NMBI, sign a formal government-level health-worker supply agreement with Ireland, set up government IELTS/OET training centres (private ones exist), introduce English-medium teaching in medical colleges and nursing institutes, form reliable public or private recruitment bodies linked to Irish hospitals, train specialists, and seek easier visa facilities.

headline_en: Chief Adviser returns home after United Arab Emirates visit
summary_en: Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus returned to Dhaka on 14 February 2025 after attending the World Governments Summit in Dubai. In meetings with UAE ministers he asked the UAE to lift the visa restrictions on Bangladeshi nationals and to recruit more Bangladeshi workers; trade, investment and an industrial park were also discussed.

facts.statement: As of mid-February 2025 the UAE had a visa ban/restriction on Bangladeshi nationals: during his visit to Dubai for the World Governments Summit, Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus called on the UAE authorities to lift the visa ban on Bangladeshi citizens and to recruit more Bangladeshi workers. The article does not report any UAE response on visas.
facts.source_in_article: Chief Adviser's Deputy Press Secretary Abul Kalam Azad Majumder, via BSS

facts.statement: Yunus met UAE Health Minister Abdur Rahman bin Mohammad Al Owais, Trade Minister Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi and other ministers; topics included lifting the visa ban on Bangladeshis, expanding bilateral trade, UAE investment plans in Chattogram port, and sport and education ties.
facts.source_in_article: Chief Adviser's Deputy Press Secretary, via BSS

facts.statement: On Thursday 13 February 2025 Yunus took part in a community engagement programme with expatriate Bangladeshis in Dubai.

UAE Trade Minister Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi proposed a special industrial park in Bangladesh for UAE businesses, to which Yunus agreed in principle; the minister said he would visit Bangladesh with a high-level trade and investment delegation in the coming months.

headline_en: Dollar price suddenly up in the open market for two reasons
summary_en: In about a week to ten days before 19 December 2024 the open-market dollar rate in Dhaka rose by at least 4 taka, and the rate banks pay for remittance dollars passed 124 taka. Bankers attribute it to December travel demand and banks buying remittance dollars at higher rates to settle import bills, and call the rise temporary.

facts.statement: In Dhaka's open (kerb) market the dollar was being bought at 126.70 taka and sold at 127.50 taka; only 10 days earlier it was bought at 122.50 taka and sold at 123 taka.

The price of remittance dollars (what banks pay for expatriate income) rose above 124 taka per dollar, because banks were buying remittance dollars at higher prices to meet travel demand and to settle import liabilities.
Banks were still selling the US dollar at 120 taka, and the rate on credit cards and other cards was kept at 120 taka, while the open-market rate was higher.

Bankers said the rise in the dollar price was temporary and that the price would return to its earlier level in January (2025). The two stated causes: sharply higher dollar demand from outbound travellers in December, and banks paying more for remittance dollars to settle import bills.

headline_en: Arabic language learning needed to raise remittances from the Middle East
summary_en: An opinion piece for World Arabic Language Day argues that Bangladeshi workers in Arab countries lose out on pay, benefits and status because they do not know Arabic, while India and Pakistan train their workers in it. It quotes a former economic counsellor at the Bangladesh Embassy in Saudi Arabia and the writer's own field observation of Bangladeshi small traders in Saudi Arabia.

facts.statement: According to a World Bank report cited in the article, expatriates sent USD 21.8 billion in remittances to Bangladesh in 2020, of which 73% came from the Gulf / Middle East. Elsewhere the same article says 80 percent of the country's remittance comes from Arabic-speaking countries (the two figures differ).
facts.source_in_article: World Bank report (first figure); writer (second figure)

facts.statement: The writer says Bangladeshi workers going to the Arab world have no prior connection with Arabic and, lacking professional Arabic skills, are deprived of proper pay, allowances and other benefits and of due status.
facts.source_in_article: Tajul Islam Kawsar, King Saud University, Riyadh (article author)

facts.statement: Researcher Md. Abu Bakar Siddique is quoted as saying that lack of language skills once caused little problem at work, but now foreign companies give priority to workers who know Arabic.

The writer says that in Saudi Arabia most Bangladeshis are seen doing low-level work because of weak Arabic, while Indian and Pakistani workers skilled in Arabic are seen being appointed to various official/office jobs; India patronises Arabic officially and Pakistan trains its citizens in Arabic.
facts.source_in_article: Tajul Islam Kawsar, King Saud University, Riyadh (article author)

facts.statement: From field work in Saudi Arabia the writer reports that Bangladeshis who open a baqala (small grocery shop) or other small businesses have to keep a Sudanese or Egyptian employee to handle daily correspondence, communication and legal formalities, paying them a large sum, which the writer says would be saved if the owner knew Arabic well.
facts.source_in_article: Tajul Islam Kawsar, King Saud University, Riyadh (article author)

facts.statement: Former Economic Counsellor and Minister at the Bangladesh Embassy in Saudi Arabia Mohammad Abul Hasan said, in a seminar paper, that the Technical and Vocational Education Department of the Islamic University of Technology (IUT) of the OIC is ready to provide Arabic language training and that online training could easily be started through the OIC university; he proposed quickly starting an online Arabic course for doctors, nurses and medical technologists to ease their way to jobs in the Arab world. This is a proposal, not an existing course.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Abul Hasan, former Economic Counsellor, Bangladesh Embassy in Saudi Arabia

facts.statement: The article cites an unnamed survey claiming that only 300 Danish citizens working in Saudi Arabia send more remittance than the thousands of Bangladeshis there do.
facts.source_in_article: an unnamed survey cited by the writer

facts.statement: The writer says the initiatives taken so far for teaching (practical) Arabic in Bangladesh are entirely inadequate.
facts.source_in_article: Tajul Islam Kawsar, King Saud University, Riyadh (article author)

key_quote_bn: তাঁরা পেশাগতভাবে আরবি ভাষায় দক্ষ না হওয়ায় যথাযোগ্য বেতন–ভাতা ও নানাবিধ সুযোগ-সুবিধা থেকে বঞ্চিত হচ্ছেন।

headline_en: Various events in Paris on AEBA's twelfth anniversary
summary_en: At its twelfth-anniversary event at its Paris headquarters on Saturday 7 December 2024, the All European Bangladesh Association (AEBA) put a set of demands (described as seven points) to Bangladesh's interim government on expatriates' rights and services.

facts.statement: The All European Bangladesh Association (AEBA), at its 12th anniversary event at its Paris headquarters, demanded of the interim government: easier issuance of visas for all EU countries from Dhaka; making every Bangladesh embassy, high commission and consulate abroad free of brokers with the highest service standard; national identity/voter ID cards for expatriates; online voting from their countries of residence; reserved parliamentary seats for expatriates; expatriate representation in the Expatriates' Welfare ministry and other relevant ministries; the right to contest elections despite dual citizenship; a government initiative from Dhaka to regularise irregular Bangladeshis abroad; and strong steps to cut migration cost and Biman Bangladesh Airlines ticket prices.
The AEBA event was chaired by AEBA president Joynul Abedin and conducted by secretary general Kazi Enayet Ullah.

headline_en: Chief Adviser seeks Singapore's help to bring back laundered money
summary_en: On 10 November 2024 Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus asked Singapore's High Commissioner Derek Loh for help in recovering money laundered from Bangladesh and in cutting the cost of recruiting Bangladeshi workers. The envoy responded positively and advised Bangladesh to digitalise its overseas recruitment system.

facts.statement: Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus urged Singapore to work with Dhaka to significantly reduce the cost of recruiting workers from Bangladesh, saying the interim government wants to cut migration costs so expatriates can send more money to their families, and proposed building 'a model framework' with Singapore for reducing recruitment cost.

Singapore's High Commissioner to Bangladesh Derek Loh gave assurance of help on recruitment cost, said Singapore is also keen to stop illegal money transactions in the recruitment process, and advised Bangladesh to digitalise its overseas recruitment system to reduce the risk of human trafficking and worker exploitation.

Yunus told the envoy that large amounts of money had been laundered from Bangladesh to many countries including Singapore and asked for Singapore's full cooperation to bring it back; the envoy promised cooperation.

headline_en: How much longer will drivers wait
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial on the BRTA driving-licence backlog says workers going abroad as drivers suffer most because they cannot leave without the smart-card licence, and some pay brokers heavily. It reports about 625,000 licences stuck at BRTA, the dispute with card supplier Madras Printers, and the interim government's decision to issue PVC cards to new applicants.

facts.statement: The editorial says outbound workers (drivers) are suffering most from the BRTA licence backlog because they cannot go abroad without the driving-licence smart card.
One driver bound for abroad applied for a licence through a broker paying 13,000 taka and had been waiting two months.

Fuzayel Ahmed, owner of a visa-processing service firm in Paltan, Dhaka, told Prothom Alo that many of his clients wait for licences and that some obtained a licence through brokers by spending 50,000 taka.
facts.source_in_article: Fuzayel Ahmed, owner of a visa-processing firm in Paltan

facts.statement: According to Prothom Alo reporting, about 625,000 (6.25 lakh) people's driving licences were stuck at BRTA. BRTA gives the applicant an application-acknowledgement paper instead of the licence, which drivers show to avoid police harassment on the road.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo news report cited in editorial

facts.statement: The interim government decided to drop the driving-licence smart card system and issue ordinary plastic polyvinyl chloride (PVC) cards. BRTA sources say PVC cards go to new applicants while old applicants get the earlier (smart) card; the PVC card can be printed quickly and will carry a QR code to verify the licence.

Card supplier Madras Printers says it cannot supply cards because BRTA is not paying its bills; BRTA says it cannot give licences because Madras Printers is not supplying cards. Under the contract the supplier was to deliver 4 million (40 lakh) cards by July 2026 but had delivered only 2 million (20 lakh) so far.

A 2021 Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) survey found 83.1 percent of households faced corruption when getting a driving licence and 83.7 percent took the service through brokers or other intermediaries.

headline_en: Thailand's e-visa for Bangladeshis to start early next year
summary_en: Thailand told Bangladesh's ambassador on 24 October 2024 that it would launch an e-visa service for Bangladeshis in early 2025. The Thai official also described the five-year Destination Thailand (DT) visa for medical travellers, warned about fake documents submitted through agents, and announced visa-free travel for official passport holders from 19 December 2024.

headline_en: 65 Bangladeshis return home from Lebanon
summary_en: On 23 October 2024 a second group of 65 Bangladeshis, including 2 newborns, returned to Dhaka from war-hit Lebanon, bringing the total to 119. A third group of 31 was due the next day via Jeddah; 1,800 Bangladeshis had registered to return, with repatriation coordinated in partnership with IOM.

facts.statement: A second batch of 65 Bangladeshis from Lebanon, including 2 newborns, landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at 5:34 pm on Wednesday 23 October 2024 on a commercial flight of Saudi Arabia, bringing the total returned from Lebanon to 119.
The first batch from Lebanon, 54 expatriate Bangladeshis including 7 children, returned on 21 October 2024.

A third batch of 31 Bangladeshis was to leave Beirut's Rafic Hariri International Airport for Jeddah on the morning of 24 October 2024 (Lebanon time) and reach Dhaka around 1 am after Thursday midnight.
A total of 1,800 Bangladeshis registered to return home from Lebanon; each of them is to be brought back in phases.
Repatriation of Bangladeshis affected by the conflict in Lebanon is being coordinated in partnership with IOM (International Organization for Migration).

headline_en: Higher study opportunities in Austria, with scholarships for bachelor's and PhD
summary_en: A detailed guide (credited to UNB) to studying in Austria for Bangladeshi students: admission requirements and intakes, the two-stage residence-permit and D-visa process through the Austrian Embassy in New Delhi, required documents and proof of funds, visa fee and timing, tuition and living costs, scholarships, part-time work rules and post-study permits.

facts.statement: At Austrian public universities study is free only for local students; foreign students proficient in German get a substantial discount on study costs. English proficiency is accepted as an alternative to German, especially for international students.
QS rankings stated: University of Vienna 137, Technical University of Vienna 190, Graz University of Technology 413, Johannes Kepler University Linz 472.

Admission requirements: a diploma or high-school certificate for a bachelor's degree; a bachelor's in the same or a relevant subject for postgraduate courses; relevant professional experience is a precondition for bachelor's degrees at universities of applied sciences; a master's programme requires at least 180 ECTS credits and a relevant bachelor's degree of at least six semesters; PhD programmes require a master's degree with research or equivalent study in the relevant field.

Austrian institutions admit students in two intakes: the winter semester starting in September and the summer semester starting in February; registration periods vary by course and are updated on each institution's website, and the whole application is done through the institution's online portal with document uploads.

Documents usually needed for admission: passport and photo or a government-issued ID copy; latest diploma/high-school or bachelor's certificate; relevant professional experience for applied-science bachelor's; English proficiency proof (IELTS, PTE Academic, TOEFL or Cambridge certificate); German proficiency proof for German-taught courses; plus anything else the institution asks for.

Some Austrian universities, especially at bachelor's level, hold an entrance exam, usually six months before the programme starts; at other levels students are assessed by online oral exam or interview (Zoom or Skype). Hand-filled papers may need to be sent by post as well as email; results and instructions come by email.
Once admission is confirmed the student is asked to pay the study fee; the offer letter and student ID are issued only after this fee is paid.

For long-term study Bangladeshi students must apply for a D-type visa, which permits a stay of more than six months. The visa should be applied for at least three to six months before classes start; the applicant should apply at least three months before entering Austria because the final decision takes time.

The process has two stages: first an application for a residence permit, then for an entry permit. The first stage is completed at the Austrian Embassy in New Delhi, India (address: EP-13, Chandragupta Marg, Chanakyapuri, New Delhi 110021, India). An appointment must be taken by email before going; on the date given in the reply the applicant attends with all papers and gives biometric data (fingerprints and photograph). The embassy sends the application directly to Austria, where the residence permit is processed.

When Austria informs the embassy that the residence permit is granted, the embassy notifies the applicant, who must apply for entry within three months of that notice; the embassy then issues a D-type visa to enter Austria, and the applicant must reach Austria and collect the residence permit within a further three months.

Documents for the Austrian student visa, with a hand-filled and signed application form: a valid passport with at least two blank pages, valid for at least three months from the day of arrival in Austria; two recent passport-size photos; offer letter from the Austrian institution; proof of sufficient funds; health insurance covering emergency treatment and travel; proof of advance accommodation in Austria. Originals plus one set of copies; any document in Bangla must be submitted with a certified German translation.
Proof of funds for the Austrian student visa: at least 6,630 euros must be shown as the minimum cost for one year. The health insurance required typically costs about 69.13 euros per month.

The overall processing cost from application until receiving the Austrian visa is 120 euros. Processing usually takes about 15 working days, but can extend to 30 to 60 working days if additional documents are needed.

Tuition: foreign students at Austrian public universities pay on average 1,452 euros a year; universities of applied sciences can cost 727 to 7,500 euros per semester; private universities usually 3,000 to 23,000 euros a year, up to 35,000 euros for some business programmes.

Living costs: a monthly budget of 900 to 1,300 euros in cities like Vienna and Salzburg (housing, food, social activities, public transport included); 900 to 1,000 euros a month in cities like Linz or Graz.

Scholarships listed: Ernst Mach Grant Worldwide (for 'graduate programme or PhD' as printed) with a monthly stipend of 1,150 euros plus up to 1,000 euros of travel cost against travel receipts; Erasmus Mundus programmes covering full tuition, visa costs, travel, insurance and monthly allowance, about 12,000 euros in all; OeAD Housing Scholarship up to 6,000 euros; University of Vienna scholarship of 12,000 euros; Joint Japan World Bank Graduate Scholarship (tuition, monthly stipend, round-trip airfare, health insurance); Austrian Development Cooperation scholarship; and the Helmut Veith Stipend for Women in Computer Science (tuition, monthly stipend).

Foreign students in Austria may do part-time jobs but need a work permit (not needed for business or freelancing). To get it they need a job offer from an Austrian business and must show the job offer letter with their residence permit. The work permit is renewable, valid one year, and allows at most 20 hours of work per week.

After graduating there are two permits for staying in Austria: a residence permit for job seekers, and the Red-White-Red Card for graduates to stay and work full time. The article says both allow graduates to work for up to one year. The job-seeker permit must be applied for before the student residence permit expires and allows at most 20 hours' work a week; the Red-White-Red Card is applied for after getting a job offer, the decision takes 15 days, and it allows up to 40 hours a week.

To cut living costs the article suggests sharing an apartment outside the city with other students (rents much lower than the centre, though far from the university), using public transport, and using the university student card, which gives notable discounts on public and private services.

headline_en: Documents attested by the Foreign Ministry will not need re-attestation in other countries: Hasan Mahmud
summary_en: On Monday 29 July 2024 in The Hague, Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud handed over Bangladesh's instrument of accession to the 1961 Apostille Convention. The ministry said documents attested by the Foreign Ministry would no longer need re-attestation abroad, that electronic apostille certificates with QR codes would be issued, and that Bangladeshis going abroad would save 500 to 600 crore taka a year; the e-APP was expected to be fully running within eight months.

facts.statement: Bangladesh was made a party to the Convention Abolishing the Requirement of Legalisation for Foreign Public Documents (Apostille Convention, 1961) at a ceremony at the Dutch Foreign Ministry in The Hague, where Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud handed over the instrument of accession. The Foreign Ministry said documents attested by Bangladesh's Foreign Ministry would 'from now on' not need to be attested again in other countries.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud / Foreign Ministry press release, 29 July 2024

facts.statement: The Foreign Ministry said the change would save Bangladeshis going abroad 500 to 600 crore taka every year.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud / Foreign Ministry press release, 29 July 2024

facts.statement: Under the e-APP (Electronic Apostille Programme) documents will be attested and an electronic apostille certificate issued, whose authenticity can be verified from anywhere in the world using the QR code on the certificate.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud / Foreign Ministry press release, 29 July 2024

facts.statement: The minister hoped that, as for other countries, the e-APP could be fully launched for Bangladeshi citizens within eight months of accession, with the final support of the other states party to the convention (so it was not yet fully operating in July 2024).
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud / Foreign Ministry press release, 29 July 2024

facts.statement: Before the change: documents such as academic certificates, birth registration certificates and marriage certificates, needed for study abroad, job applications, settling abroad or marrying a foreign national, had to be attested by several Bangladeshi ministries and the Foreign Ministry, and then again by the foreign embassy, the destination country's foreign ministry and other foreign authorities, which was time-consuming, laborious and costly.

headline_en: 5 Bangladeshis killed in Dubai: 'Bring my Raju back, let me see his face once'
summary_en: Five Bangladeshi workers employed by the same firm were killed on the spot when their vehicle exploded on the way to work in Dubai at about 7:30 am local time on Sunday 7 July 2024. Four were from Balenga village in Nawabganj upazila, Dhaka, and one from Dohar; the report describes the grieving families and the debts taken to send the men abroad.

facts.statement: Five Bangladeshis were killed on the spot when a vehicle exploded while they were going to their workplace in Dubai at about 7:30 am local time on Sunday 7 July 2024; all five worked at the same establishment. Four were from Balenga village, Joykrishnapur union, Nawabganj upazila, Dhaka, and one from the Dohar Bazar area of Dohar upazila.

The dead were: Md. Rana (30), son of Lutfor Rahman; Md. Rashed (32), son of Abdul Hakim; Md. Raju (24), son of Sheikh Irshad; Ibadul Islam (34), son of Sheikh Ibrahim, all of Balenga village; and Md. Hira Mia (22), son of Md. Manjur, of Dohar Bazar.
Ibadul Islam's mother Nazma Begum took 1.5 lakh taka from an NGO a year before to send her son to Dubai; she said she must still bear the instalments although he has died.
facts.source_in_article: Nazma Begum, mother of the deceased

facts.statement: Md. Rashed's mother Yaron Begum sent him abroad on borrowed money and the debt had not yet been repaid when he died; he was the family's only earner.
The families appealed for the bodies to be brought home; the article reports no information on repatriation of the bodies, the employer's name or compensation.

headline_en: Crowd catches SI while robbing gold from Saudi-returned expatriate
summary_en: On Sunday 19 May 2024 in Chattogram, an off-duty police sub-inspector of Khulshi police station and two associates stopped the car of a Saudi-returned expatriate coming from Shah Amanat International Airport and took 16 bhori of gold from him. Bystanders caught the SI and one associate on a flyover; the SI was suspended and a case was being filed.

facts.statement: At about 3 pm on Sunday 19 May 2024, Saudi expatriate Abdul Khalek (also printed as Mohammad Khalek) was returning from Chattogram Shah Amanat International Airport when his vehicle was stopped at Khulshi Tiger Pass by Sub-Inspector Aminul Islam of Khulshi police station with two associates, who snatched 16 bhori of gold from him, drove him around the city in the vehicle and tried to drop him off on the Akhtaruzzaman Chowdhury flyover.
facts.source_in_article: Panchlaish police station OC Santosh Kumar Chakma

facts.statement: The expatriate held on to the officer's clothes, a crowd gathered and Panchlaish police detained SI Aminul Islam and associate Shahidul Islam Jahed (45) of KB Aman Ali Road, Rahattar Pool, Bakalia; a third man fled. The SI, who was not on duty, was temporarily suspended and a case was being filed against him at the police station.
facts.source_in_article: CMP Deputy Commissioner (North) Mokhlesur Rahman; Khulshi OC Sheikh Neyamat Ullah

named_actors.name: Aminul Islam
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Police sub-inspector accused of robbing 16 bhori of gold from a Saudi-returned expatriate while off duty, with two associates.
named_actors.status: detained, temporarily suspended; case being filed (19 May 2024)

named_actors.name: Shahidul Islam Jahed (45)
named_actors.location: KB Aman Ali Road, Rahattar Pool, Bakalia, Chattogram
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Associate of SI Aminul Islam in the gold robbery.

people_cases.who: Abdul Khalek (also printed Mohammad Khalek), Saudi expatriate
people_cases.what_happened: Robbed of 16 bhori of gold by an off-duty police SI and two associates after leaving Shah Amanat airport; driven around the city and nearly dumped on a flyover.
people_cases.outcome: He held on to the officer; crowd and police detained two of the three; whether the gold was recovered is not stated.

key_quote_bn: দুই সহযোগীকে নিয়ে তিনি প্রবাসী আবদুল খালেকের কাছ থেকে ১৬ ভরি সোনা ছিনিয়ে নেন।

headline_en: Attacks on foreigners in Kyrgyzstan, Bangladeshi students in panic
summary_en: After a clash on 13 May 2024 between a few locals and Egyptian medical students in Bishkek, locals began attacking foreigners, including Bangladeshi, Pakistani and Indian students and workers; Bangladeshi students told Prothom Alo they were hiding and wanted to go home. Bangladesh has no embassy in Kyrgyzstan; the embassy in Uzbekistan covers it, estimates 600-800 students and about a thousand workers there, and told students to stay indoors.

facts.statement: On 13 May 2024 two or three local residents clashed with some Egyptian medical university students in Bishkek; attacks on foreigners in Bishkek then began, which the article dates to the night of 16 May, while a student quoted says attacks began on the evening of Friday (17 May). Bangladeshi, Pakistani and Indian students were attacked, foreigners were beaten house to house, property was vandalised and attackers entered medical college hostels.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladeshi students and others, to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The article says at least 800 Bangladeshi medical students are in Kyrgyzstan; the Bangladesh Embassy (in Uzbekistan) has no statistics on how many Bangladeshis are there but estimates 600 to 800 students and about a thousand workers.
facts.source_in_article: reporter; Bangladesh Embassy in Uzbekistan estimate

facts.statement: Bangladesh has no embassy in Kyrgyzstan; the Bangladesh Embassy in Uzbekistan is responsible for Kyrgyzstan. The ambassador said a number is kept open for round-the-clock contact with the embassy (the number is not printed).
facts.source_in_article: Ambassador to Uzbekistan Mohammad Monirul Islam

facts.statement: The embassy told Bangladeshi students in Kyrgyzstan not to leave their homes; the university authority (Royal Metropolitan Medical University, Bishkek) told students not to go outside their rooms.
facts.source_in_article: Ambassador Mohammad Monirul Islam; student Syed Rakibul Islam

facts.statement: Students said Bangladeshi workers and students were injured in the attacks, but no one could give a number; the ambassador said that as of 18 May 2024 there was no information of any Bangladeshi being injured or killed, and that Kyrgyzstan's foreign ministry said the situation was under control. (The two accounts differ.)
facts.source_in_article: Bangladeshi students; Ambassador Mohammad Monirul Islam

facts.statement: Bangladeshi students said social-media apps were being used to locate foreign students, locals were patrolling the city in convoys of 20-25 cars, students of various countries were hiding in groups of 15-20 in a room, and police deployed across the city failed to control the situation. There were also allegations of abuse of female foreign students.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladeshi students; videos sent by students

facts.statement: Third-year student Syed Rakibul Islam of Royal Metropolitan Medical University, Bishkek, said he had gone nearly two days without food while in hiding and wanted to return to Bangladesh; Saima Kabir, second-semester student at Kyrgyz State Medical Academy, said locals were attacking foreign students and workers, that her hostel was not safe with angry locals outside, and asked for security help.
facts.source_in_article: students Syed Rakibul Islam and Saima Kabir

people_cases.who: Syed Rakibul Islam, third-year student, Royal Metropolitan Medical University, Bishkek
people_cases.what_happened: In hiding since attacks on foreigners began; nearly two days without food.
people_cases.outcome: Wants to return to Bangladesh; still in hiding on 18 May 2024.

people_cases.who: Saima Kabir, second-semester student, Kyrgyz State Medical Academy
people_cases.what_happened: Says her hostel is unsafe with angry locals outside attacking any foreigner.

key_quote_bn: দূতাবাসের ধারণা, ৬০০ থেকে ৮০০ শিক্ষার্থী আর হাজারখানেকের মতো শ্রমিক কিরগিজস্তানে রয়েছেন।
